blocks.text: The last lesson introduced magnitude, the length of a vector. This lesson asks the opposite question: what if you want to keep only the direction a vector points in, and throw away its length entirely? The answer is a unit vector.

blocks.alt: A vector being normalized by dividing by its own magnitude, producing a unit vector of length 1
blocks.caption: The whole lesson in one picture: normalize to strip away length.

blocks.text: 1. What a Unit Vector Is

A unit vector is any vector whose magnitude is exactly 1. The word "unit" just means "one". Nothing else about a unit vector is special or restricted, it can point in any direction at all, the only requirement is that its length equals 1.

blocks.title: Direction, with size stripped away
blocks.content: Because every unit vector has the same length, the only thing left that can differ between them is direction. A unit vector is a clean way to talk about "which way something points" without the length getting in the way of the comparison.

blocks.text: It is worth contrasting this with the previous lesson one more time. Magnitude answers how long, unit vectors answer which way, and together the two of them are a complete description of any vector at all, split cleanly into two independent, separately useful pieces.

This single requirement, magnitude exactly 1, is easy to state but worth double checking in real code with a tolerance rather than an exact equality check, since floating point arithmetic almost never produces a magnitude of precisely 1.0 down to the last decimal, even for a mathematically perfect unit vector.
1.1 The Standard Basis: Two Named Unit Vectors

Two specific unit vectors are so common they get their own names: e_x = (1, 0), pointing one step along the x-axis, and e_y = (0, 1), pointing one step along the y-axis. Together they are called the standard basis.

blocks.alt: Two unit vectors, e_x pointing right along the x-axis and e_y pointing up along the y-axis, both length 1
blocks.caption: These two short arrows are the building blocks every other 2D vector can be built from.

blocks.text: Higher dimensions have their own standard basis too, just with more named vectors, e_x, e_y, e_z, and so on, one for each axis, each one a 1 in a single position and 0 everywhere else. Nothing about the idea changes, there are simply more of them to keep track of.
2. Turning Any Vector Into a Unit Vector
The process of converting any vector into a unit vector pointing the exact same way is called normalizing. The rule is simple: divide every component of the vector by the vector's own magnitude.

code.content:
v = [4, 3]
magnitude = (4**2 + 3**2) ** 0.5   # 5.0
unit_v = [4 / magnitude, 3 / magnitude]
print(unit_v)   # [0.8, 0.6]

blocks.alt: The original vector of length 5 shown dashed in grey, with the unit vector of length 1 pointing the same direction shown solid in blue
blocks.caption: The unit vector points exactly the same way as the original, just cut down to a length of 1.

blocks.text: Checking the result confirms it worked: the magnitude of [0.8, 0.6] is the square root of 0.8 squared plus 0.6 squared, which is the square root of 0.64 plus 0.36, which is the square root of exactly 1. A length of 1, pointing the same direction as the original vector [4, 3].

code.content:
import numpy as np
v = np.array([4, 3])
unit_v = v / np.linalg.norm(v)
print(unit_v)                 # [0.8 0.6]
print(np.linalg.norm(unit_v)) # 1.0

blocks.text: It is worth double checking a normalized result at least once with real numbers rather than trusting the code blindly the first time you use it in a new context. A quick print of np.linalg.norm on the result, confirming it lands on 1.0, catches a shape mistake or a units mistake far earlier than discovering it several steps later in a pipeline.
2.1 Any Vector as a Combination of Unit Vectors
Once e_x and e_y exist, any 2D vector can be described as a scaled combination of the two. The vector (4, 3) is nothing more than 4 copies of e_x plus 3 copies of e_y, added together.

blocks.alt: The vector (4, 3) shown as 4 steps along e_x followed by 3 steps along e_y
blocks.caption: Scaling and adding two unit vectors is enough to reach any point in the plane.

code.content:
e_x = np.array([1, 0])
e_y = np.array([0, 1])
v = 4 * e_x + 3 * e_y
print(v)   # [4 3]

blocks.text: This is worth sitting with, because it is the same idea, scalar multiplication and vector addition, from earlier lessons in this module, just applied specifically to unit vectors. It is also the exact idea behind a basis, covered in full in a later lesson: a small set of reference vectors that every other vector can be built from.
2.2 Why This Decomposition Is Useful

Breaking a vector down into scaled unit vectors is not just a tidy way to write it, it is how a lot of vector reasoning actually gets done in practice. Instead of asking what does this whole complicated vector mean, it becomes possible to ask a simpler, separate question for each axis: how much of this vector points in the x direction, and how much points in the y direction, then combine those two simpler answers back together.

This same reasoning is exactly what makes matrix multiplication, covered later in this module, work the way it does. A matrix acting on a vector can be understood one basis direction at a time, which is a far more manageable way to think about it than trying to hold the entire transformation in your head all at once.
3. The Unit Circle Connection

Picture every possible unit vector in 2D, one pointing right, one pointing up, one pointing diagonally, and every direction in between. Every single one of them ends at a point exactly 1 unit from the origin. Trace all of those endpoints together and they form a perfect circle of radius 1, centered on the origin, usually called the unit circle.

blocks.alt: Several unit vectors pointing in different directions, all reaching exactly to the edge of a circle of radius 1
blocks.caption: No matter which direction a unit vector points, its tip always lands somewhere on this same circle.

blocks.text: This is also where the trigonometry you may already know quietly connects to vectors: a 2D unit vector at some angle can always be written as (cos angle, sin angle). You do not need trigonometry to work with unit vectors day to day, but it is worth knowing this connection exists, since it is exactly what later shows up when measuring the angle between two vectors.

The same circle idea extends to 3 dimensions too, where it becomes a sphere of radius 1 instead of a circle, and every 3D unit vector lands somewhere on the surface of that sphere. Past 3 dimensions the shape is still called a sphere, just a higher-dimensional one nobody can actually picture, though the defining property, every point exactly 1 unit from the origin, stays exactly the same.
3.1 Unit Vectors and Angles
Picking a specific angle turns the cosine and sine connection from the last section into an actual, computable unit vector. A unit vector at 30 degrees works out to a concrete pair of numbers.

blocks.alt: A single unit vector drawn at a 30 degree angle from the x-axis, landing on the unit circle
blocks.caption: The angle alone is enough information to compute exactly where this vector points.

code.content:
import math
angle_degrees = 30
angle_radians = math.radians(angle_degrees)
unit_v = [math.cos(angle_radians), math.sin(angle_radians)]
print(unit_v)   # about [0.866, 0.5]

blocks.text: This angle-based way of writing a unit vector becomes especially useful once you need to describe rotation, gradually turning a vector by changing its angle while keeping its length fixed at exactly 1. That specific use case belongs to a later lesson, but the cos and sin building blocks needed for it are exactly what was just introduced here.
4. Why Bother Removing the Length
This is not a purely academic exercise, it is exactly what "normalizing an embedding" means in practice, a phrase you will run into constantly once you start working with real embedding models.

items: Once every embedding in a collection has magnitude 1, comparing them becomes purely a comparison of direction, which is what actually reflects meaning.
Several popular embedding models already return unit-normalized vectors by default, or explicitly recommend normalizing before comparing them.
Cosine similarity, covered properly in a later lesson, becomes a simpler calculation once both vectors involved are already unit vectors.

blocks.text: It is worth being honest that normalizing does throw information away on purpose. If the original magnitude carried meaning, for example a confidence score encoded as vector length, normalizing erases that on purpose in exchange for a cleaner direction-only comparison. Whether that trade is the right one depends entirely on whether the specific system cares about magnitude at all.

A useful habit is asking, before normalizing anything, whether the length of this specific vector was ever meant to carry information in the first place. If the answer is no, normalizing is close to a free simplification. If the answer is yes, it is worth pausing and being deliberate about the trade being made.
5. The One Vector You Cannot Normalize

The all-zero vector, [0, 0] or its equivalent in any number of dimensions, has a magnitude of exactly 0. Normalizing means dividing by the magnitude, and dividing by 0 is not defined, so the zero vector has no unit vector version at all. Real code needs to guard against this edge case explicitly.

In practice, an all-zero embedding is rare but not impossible, it can happen if an input produces no meaningful signal at all for a given model. Production systems that normalize embeddings routinely include exactly the kind of zero-check shown above, precisely because this edge case does eventually show up at scale even though it looks unlikely for any single vector.
6. Normalizing a Higher-Dimensional Vector

Nothing about normalizing changes once a vector has more than 2 or 3 components. The same divide-by-the-magnitude rule applies, whether the vector describes a point on a page or a real word embedding with hundreds of numbers.

code.content:
embedding = np.array([0.12, -0.48, 0.91, 0.03])
unit_embedding = embedding / np.linalg.norm(embedding)
print(np.linalg.norm(unit_embedding))   # 1.0, no matter how many dimensions it started with

blocks.text: This is precisely the step many embedding pipelines run right after generating an embedding, before storing it anywhere, so that every vector in the collection is guaranteed to be comparable on equal footing.

It is worth explicitly noticing what did not change between the earlier 2D example and this one: the code is identical in shape, divide by np.linalg.norm, the only difference is how many numbers happen to be inside the array being divided.
6.1 Checking the Work
Whenever normalizing feels uncertain, the fastest sanity check is always the same: compute the norm of the result and confirm it equals 1, allowing for a tiny amount of floating-point rounding error.

code.content:
result = embedding / np.linalg.norm(embedding)
assert abs(np.linalg.norm(result) - 1.0) < 1e-9, "normalization failed"

blocks.text: 7. A Worked Example
Normalize vector B from the earlier lessons, (1, 5), and compare it side by side with the original.

code.content:
b = np.array([1, 5])
unit_b = b / np.linalg.norm(b)
print(unit_b)                 # about [0.196, 0.981]
print(np.linalg.norm(unit_b)) # 1.0

blocks.text: Notice the unit vector still leans almost straight upward, just like the original B did, since normalizing never changes direction. All that changed is the length, shrunk down to exactly 1.

Notice this is the exact same pair of vectors, A and B, that have appeared throughout this Math and Statistics module so far, first as plain coordinates, then measured for magnitude, and now normalized. Watching the same two vectors move through each lesson is a good way to see how these ideas stack on top of one another rather than existing as separate, unrelated topics.
8. Normalizing Many Vectors at Once
Real code rarely normalizes just one vector at a time, it normalizes an entire matrix of embeddings in one step, one row at a time.

blocks.alt: A flow diagram showing a matrix of raw embeddings having the norm of each row computed, then each row divided by its own norm, producing a matrix of unit embeddings
blocks.caption: The same normalizing rule from earlier in this lesson, just applied to every row of a matrix at once.

code.content:
embeddings = np.array([
    [4, 3],
    [1, 5],
    [0.12, -0.48],
])
row_norms = np.linalg.norm(embeddings, axis=1, keepdims=True)
unit_embeddings = embeddings / row_norms
print(np.linalg.norm(unit_embeddings, axis=1))   # [1. 1. 1.]

blocks.text: The axis=1, keepdims=True detail is what tells NumPy to compute one norm per row rather than one norm for the entire matrix, and to keep that result shaped so it divides each row correctly instead of the whole matrix at once. Getting this one detail wrong is one of the most common real bugs in embedding pipelines.
8.1 A Common Bug: Normalizing the Whole Matrix at Once

Leaving out axis=1 is one of the easiest mistakes to make here, and it does not throw an error, it just silently produces the wrong answer. Without it, NumPy computes a single norm for the entire matrix rather than one per row, and every row ends up divided by the same shared number instead of its own.

blocks.title: Why this is dangerous
blocks.content: Code with this bug still runs successfully and still returns a matrix that looks reasonable at a glance, which is exactly what makes it dangerous. The only way to catch it is checking that np.linalg.norm on each individual row of the result actually comes out to 1, not just eyeballing the output.

blocks.text: 9. Practice: Normalize These by Hand
Try normalizing (6, 8) by hand before checking the answer below.

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.content: The magnitude of (6, 8) is the square root of 36 plus 64, which is the square root of 100, which is exactly 10. Dividing each component by 10 gives the unit vector (0.6, 0.8). Checking it: 0.6 squared plus 0.8 squared is 0.36 plus 0.64, which is exactly 1.

blocks.text: If you want an extra check on your work, try normalizing (5, 12) as well. The magnitude works out to 13, since 5 squared plus 12 squared is 25 plus 144, which is 169, and the square root of 169 is 13, giving a unit vector of (5/13, 12/13).

These clean examples, where the magnitude comes out to a whole number, were chosen deliberately to make hand verification easy. Real embeddings rarely have this property, their magnitudes are typically long, irregular decimals, which is exactly why real normalization work always happens in code rather than by hand.
10. Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to guard against the zero vector before normalizing, which crashes with a division by zero in real code.
Assuming normalizing changes what a vector means, it only removes the length, the direction is always preserved exactly.
Confusing a unit vector with a vector that simply has small components, magnitude exactly 1 is a precise requirement, not just small.
Re-normalizing an already-unit vector and expecting something to change, dividing a unit vector by its own magnitude of 1 leaves it exactly as it was.
Forgetting axis=1 and keepdims=True when normalizing a whole matrix of embeddings row by row, silently producing incorrect results.
Normalizing a vector that intentionally encodes meaning in its magnitude, like a confidence score, and losing that information without realizing it.

blocks.text: Key Takeaway

A unit vector is any vector with magnitude exactly 1, pure direction with the length stripped away. Normalizing means dividing a vector by its own magnitude, and the result always points the exact same way as the original, just shrunk or stretched to a length of 1. The one exception is the all-zero vector, which cannot be normalized at all, since that would mean dividing by a magnitude of 0.

Every possible unit vector lands somewhere on the unit circle, one radius away from the origin, and this same idea extends cleanly to embeddings with hundreds of dimensions. Normalized embeddings show up constantly in real AI systems, specifically because once every vector has the same length, comparing them becomes purely a comparison of direction, which is what actually reflects meaning.
